extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimental scientists, and students of scientific method (readers of Bacon's Novum Organum)
extracted.subtask_description: A program of practical rules and classes of 'instances' (examples/experiments) for discovering natural powers and causes via induction. Emphasises how to render imperceptible phenomena perceptible, how to observe processes, and which kinds of experiments are most informative for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of imperceptible bodies to the sensible sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: All delicate experiments on natural or artificial bodies, by which the genuine are distinguished from the adulterated, and the better from the more common, should be referred to this division; for they bring that which is not the object of the senses within their sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrivances and delicate experiments (example: spirits of wine in a vial heated to produce vapor expanding a bladder) to measure how much of a substance becomes aëriform and the expansion it undergoes. Prefer small-scale, careful procedures to violent or crude separations; avoid methods that superinduce new qualities (e.g., vapors produced chiefly by the fire rather than pre-existing in the water). Seek skilful separations (distillations) that imitate rather than destroy natural conformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermometric detection of insensible heat or cold
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat or cold of such a degree as not to be sensible from its weakness are rendered sensible by the thermometer; for the cold and heat are not actually perceived by the touch, but heat expands and cold contracts the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure expansion/contraction (first reduction to sight) rather than rely on direct tactile perception when sensations are too slight; use instruments (thermometer) that translate an imperceptible quality into a visible change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of artificial separations to detect constituent mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixture of bodies (how much aqueous, oleaginous or spirituous, ashy or salt parts they contain) is rendered sensible by artificial and skilful separations in tangible substances; the nature of the spirit in them, though not immediately perceptible, is discovered by the various motions and efforts of bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ distillation and separations but be cautious: many current methods are 'mere guesses and blind attempts' that use violent heat and destroy delicate conformations. Observe that processes may superinduce qualities; interpret results knowing the method's influence on the sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of experimental artefacts (superinduced qualities)
rubrics_metrics.description: In attacking bodies by fire, or other methods, many qualities are superinduced by the fire itself, and the other bodies used to effect the separation, which were not originally in the compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for qualities created by the experimental procedure (e.g., vapor emitted from water by fire may be chiefly created by expansion). Design experiments and interpret results recognizing intervention effects of method and agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure motions as time (action of sense is motion/time)
rubrics_metrics.description: The action of the sense takes place by motion, and this motion is time. If the motion of any body be either so slow or so swift as not to be proportioned to the necessary momentum which operates on the senses, the object is not perceived at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For motions imperceptible from slowness use accumulation over time; for those imperceptible from velocity, devise means to measure or slow them (Galilean-style timing experiments). Recognise time as fundamental in perceiving and measuring natural action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attenuation or deadening to reduce overpowering objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The action of a powerful object may be reduced to the sensible sphere by removing the object to a greater distance, or by deadening its effects by the interposition of a medium, or by the admission of its reflection where the direct impression is too strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a stimulus is too strong for senses (e.g., sun's glare), weaken it via distance, medium, or reflection to observe properties without destruction or sensory overload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of other animals' senses as substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes this reduction is not extended to the senses of man, but to those of some other animal, whose senses, in some points, exceed those of man (e.g., dog for scents; cat, owl for night light).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use animals with superior modalities to detect phenomena inaccessible to humans, but interpret analogically and with caution about differences in sensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid defining objects only in relation to man (correct anthropocentrism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Senses' deceptions which make them define objects in their relation to man, and not in their relation to the universe, are only corrected by universal reasoning and philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement sensory data with universal reasoning; do not mistake human sensory limits for universal properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the road/itinerant/jointed (observe gradual processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: They indicate the gradually continued motions of nature. One should not merely see materials and finished work, but be present while nature is at labour and proceeding with its work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe natural processes continuously (examples: observe seed germination daily; observe hatching eggs; study formation from putrefaction). Watch in-progress phenomena to capture the sequence and transitions, not only initial and final states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary/substitutive instances by approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution by approximation: when appropriate instances are lacking, a medium may be found which deadens an effect more than another comparatively and in degree (example: magnet attracting iron through various media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use graded or comparative intermediates to approximate inaccessible conditions; perform comparative experiments to infer limits and degrees of effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary/substitutive instances by analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution by analogy serves to reduce that which is not the object of the senses by considering some similar perceptible body (example: analogy between mixtures of oil/water and mixtures of flame/air in spirits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies between perceptible and imperceptible systems to generate hypotheses, but 'adopt with some judgment'—analogical substitution is less sure than direct instances and must be tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lancing/twitching instances (instances of Democritus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances which warn the understanding of the admirable and exquisite subtilty of nature, so that it becomes roused and awakened to attention, observation, and proper inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect striking, paradoxical, or minute examples (ink forming many letters, saffron coloring a tub of water, a little musk perfuming a large air). Use them to provoke hypotheses and attention to subtle, large-ranging effects of small causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of lancing instances
rubrics_metrics.description: In the cases pointed out, one action does not disturb or impede another of a different nature, yet those of a similar nature subdue and extinguish each other (e.g., sun's light overcomes candle, strong perfume overcomes delicate one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using lancing instances, also determine their limits and interactions: test where actions coexist, where one dominates, and how similar actions interfere; include such boundary observations among inductive supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical instances: mathematical/measure and propitious/benevolent
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice is defective by being deceptive (powers ill-defined) or too laborious. Powers are defined by space, time, quantity, or predominance—these four must be considered (mathematical instances and instances of measure). Propitious/benevolent instances direct practice to what matters and lessen instruments or matter required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In applied work, always quantify space, time, dose, and dominance. Seek instances that reduce resource requirements or focus on humanity's chief concerns; balance theoretical thoroughness with practical economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the rod/rule (completion/non ultrà) — measure by space/distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers and motions of bodies act through limited and certain spaces; it is of great importance to practice that these should be understood and noted in every nature which is investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the definite distances/radii within which powers act (examples: contact-only powers like touch; magnetic attraction within a narrow sphere; possible terrestrial magnetic force). Note limits depend on mass, vigour of powers, medium. Apply for both short and long-range powers, projectiles, and instruments (telescopes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of expansion/compression (spherical motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: In our measure of this motion we must inquire what degree of compression or extension bodies easily and readily admit of, according to their nature, and at what point they begin to resist it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform experiments to determine compressibility and extensibility (examples: air in a glass egg drawn by suction; leaden globe of water hammered/pressed until water exudes). Distinguish behaviour of rare bodies (air) from tangible ones (water, metals) and note failure modes (bursting, breaking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the course/water instances (measure by time/moments)
rubrics_metrics.description: They measure nature by the moments of time. All motion or natural action takes place in time; even apparently instantaneous actions admit of greater or less rapidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify durations and temporal order (examples: heavenly returns, tides, projectile and animal motion, light vs sound delays). Use relative timing (light faster than sound) and first/last extraction principles (infusion/distillation order) to design and interpret experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of quantity (doses of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: They measure the powers by the quantity of bodies, and point out the effect of the quantity in the degree of power. Some powers only subsist in universal quantity; almost all particular powers act according to the greater or less quantity of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine exact proportions required for effects (do not assume linear scaling). Examples: small vs large casks affecting fermentation; amount of magnet vs attracted iron; baths vs sprinkling effects. Guard against vague estimates—measure experimentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrestling instances (instances of predominance)
rubrics_metrics.description: They point out the predominance and submission of powers compared with each other, and which of them is more energetic or inferior; motions and effects are compounded, decomposed and combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comparative/competitive experiments to see which power dominates in mixtures or interactions. Systematically enumerate principal kinds of motions (to compare relative strength) as a route to defining predominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of primary active motions: resistance of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: First motion: the resistance of matter, which exists in every particle, and completely prevents its annihilation; exemplified by the axiom that two bodies cannot exist in the same place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat resistance as a fundamental motion to be considered in all experiments and in assessing limits, breakage, or persistence of particles under forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of primary active motions: motion of connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Second motion: the motion of connection, by which bodies do not allow themselves to be separated at any point from the contact of another body; this is called by the schools a motion to prevent a vacuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider adhesive/connate tendencies among bodies when designing interventions or separations; include tests for cohesion and the tendency to maintain contact.
